title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Medical equipment cleaning (external only)
audience: Owners of small Australian businesses that clean the external surfaces of medical equipment in clinics and care settings, who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, including collection and release time, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with the owner's own records.
Set a minimum charge for short single-item jobs, and explain it to a facility before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: The rate depends on the cost of running the business, the care needed to clean items without damaging them, how many items a batch holds, the travel and access involved, and what you can show from your own records. Work that needs the facility's release process or after-hours access can justify a higher rate, but only where your own costs show it. The research found no medical-equipment rate, so do not copy a rate from a competitor or from a general cleaning source. Set the rate from your own costs and billable hours.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Travel between sites, collection and return of items, waiting for a release, quoting, admin, training, PPE and equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Subtract them from paid hours. For example, if 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours must be recovered from the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week. Billable time is often about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours (Jobber, last modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, so check your own log against it.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, PPE, training, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (1 October 2026), so decide how each will be allowed for. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by the billable hours to reach the base rate. Business Victoria advises reviewing prices about every three months (no date shown on the page).

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A short job, such as one trolley or a single cabinet, can cost more in time than it earns, because travel, collection and set-up do not shrink with the size of the item. A minimum charge covers the time to attend and start work. A contractor pricing guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, setup and cleanup (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Its figures are labelled illustrative: $105 of visit cost at a 30 per cent target margin gives a $150 minimum. Use the method, not the figure. The research found no medical-equipment minimum charge, so set and state your own minimum in writing before the visit.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, collection, admin, training, PPE time and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, PPE, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, collection, set-up and admin for a short job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: A one-person external equipment business pays for 40 hours a week, but only about 24 of those hours can be billed, because travel between clinics, collection of items and admin take the rest. The owner plans to set the rate as if all 40 hours were billable.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the 40-hour assumption is kept, and what should be done instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if all 40 paid hours were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. At 24 billable hours out of 40, which is 60 per cent, the rate has to be about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week. The rate must be built from billable hours, then compared with the owner's own records and checked against the minimum charge before it is published. The research found no medical-equipment rate to compare it with.

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from the owner's own costs and billable hours, then compare it with the owner's own records.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short single-item jobs at the same rate, without covering travel and collection.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, collection, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The research for this course did not retrieve a current ACCC source on minimum or call-out charges, or on what counts as a fair term. Check current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet to a facility.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave and superannuation with a registered tax agent. This lesson gives no tax advice.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with the owner's own records.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against the owner's own records.
Set and state a minimum charge for short jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short jobs?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week
